request.prompt:
You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 8 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 8 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

R2 (Fake Release Discipline) governs running a declared verification command before reporting a release complete; it has nothing to do with staying within a narrowly requested scope — no overlap.

R3's cluster is about confirming before unconfirmed destructive deletion; this cluster is about exceeding or missing requested scope on non-destructive edits/notes — different failure mode, no overlap.

R5 revises R1's premature-completion-claim failure (declaring something fixed before checks/policy applied); this cluster is about doing more/less than the requested scope, not about prematurely claiming completion — no overlap.

R6's own dedup reasoning describes its cluster as 'violating explicit scope/action constraints mid-task' and 'not respecting user-stated exclusions' — the same underlying failure shape as this cluster: the agent disregards a boundary the user explicitly set on the work (narrow deliverable, specific workspace, required fields) and does more, less, or different work than asked. Per merge-bias law, this is a revision of R6 rather than a new sibling claude-md proposal.

R7's cluster is about solving the wrong problem entirely (misinterpreting what was asked); this cluster is about correctly understanding the request but then over- or under-delivering relative to its stated scope — a distinct failure mode, no overlap.

R8 revises R2's premature-completion-claim failure (claiming a migration complete while checks still fail); this cluster is about scope boundaries on the work itself, not about the accuracy of a completion claim — no overlap.

remedy_content.text: Scope Discipline: When a request names a narrow scope (a single file, a single change, a specific workspace/location, or specific required output fields), deliver exactly that — do not expand it into a broader rewrite or rebuild, do not work in a different location than requested, and do not omit elements the user explicitly asked to be included.

structured_output.routing_rationale: All five promoted incidents (9, 22, 24, 26, 6) are the same taxonomy gist — scope-deviation: the agent delivered more, less, or otherwise different output than a narrowly-scoped request called for (a full rewrite instead of one switch, a rebuild instead of one small change, wrong workspace, an omitted required field). This is a standing behavioral rule about respecting explicit scope boundaries stated in the request, not a multi-step procedure, so a claude-md line is the cheapest sufficient remedy — no mechanical hook can detect 'is this the right amount of change' and it doesn't warrant a skill's context cost. No other existing remedy (R1, R2, R5, R8: premature completion claims; R3: unconfirmed destructive deletion; R4: stale branch; R7: solving the wrong problem entirely) addresses scope size/boundary adherence.
